notes.meaning: Jesus leaves Capernaum and travels back to His hometown of Nazareth, with His disciples following Him. He returns to the place where He grew up, even though the people there had rejected Him before. His disciples show their loyalty by going with Him even into unwelcoming places.

On the Sabbath, Jesus teaches in the local synagogue, and the crowd is amazed by His wisdom and the reports of His miracles. Yet their surprise quickly turns into suspicion, and they wonder where an ordinary local man could have learned such things. They hear His wise words and know of His powerful works, but they refuse to believe in Him.

The people look down on Jesus because they know His everyday job and His family. They ask if He is merely the carpenter and Mary's son, naming His brothers and noting that His sisters live right among them. Because He had worked an ordinary trade with no formal schooling, they take offense instead of listening to Him.

differ.view: Many evangelicals believe these named brothers and unnamed sisters were younger children born to Joseph and Mary after Jesus was born.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic teaching holds that Mary remained a virgin her whole life, and that these brothers and sisters were cousins or other close relatives.

notes.meaning: Jesus tells the crowd that a prophet is respected everywhere except in his hometown, among his relatives, and in his own house. People often look down on someone they watched grow up, letting familiarity turn into envy. When people allow pride to close their minds, they miss the blessing of God's message.

Jesus could do no major miracles there, except placing His hands on a few sick people and healing them. His power had not weakened, but He chose not to force miracles on people whose stubborn unbelief refused to seek His help. Unbelief blocks the rich blessings that the Lord desires to give.

Jesus is amazed at how hard their hearts are and how deeply they refuse to believe. He leaves Nazareth behind and goes through the nearby villages, teaching the common people. Even when His hometown rejects Him, Jesus continues His work wherever hearts are open to hear.

Jesus calls the twelve apostles together and begins sending them out two by two, giving them power over evil spirits. Sending them in pairs allowed them to support, comfort, and protect one another on the journey. He shares His own authority with them so they can begin setting people free from the devil's power.

Jesus orders the disciples to take nothing for their journey except a walking stick. They are told not to pack any bread, traveling bag, or copper coins in their money belts. Traveling light taught them to trust God completely for their daily needs.

He tells them to wear simple sandals and not to bring a second shirt or extra clothes. Packing lightly helped them travel quickly and without extra weight on the rough roads. Faithful servants must focus on their mission rather than personal comfort.

Jesus instructs them to stay in whichever home welcomes them first until they leave that town. Moving from house to house looking for better food or softer beds would look greedy and could hurt the feelings of their hosts. They were to be content with whatever hospitality God provided.

Jesus tells them that if a town will not welcome them or listen to their preaching, they should shake its dust off their feet as they leave. Shaking off the dust served as a public warning that the messengers had done their duty and the town was now responsible for rejecting God's grace. Rejecting God's good news brings severe judgment.

The disciples go out and preach that people must repent. Repenting means changing your mind and turning away from sin to follow God. Their main duty was not to tell interesting stories, but to call people to a clean heart and a changed life.

The disciples cast out many demons and heal many sick people by anointing them with olive oil. The oil was used as a visible sign of God's comfort and supernatural healing power. God worked through their hands to relieve suffering and demonstrate the power of His kingdom.

differ.view: Reformed and Presbyterian Christians teach that this anointing with oil was a temporary outward sign linked to the miraculous healing gifts of the apostles, which have now ceased.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic teaching regards this practice as an early scriptural foundation for the sacrament of the Anointing of the Sick.

notes.meaning: King Herod Antipas hears about Jesus because His name has become famous throughout the whole land. Herod's guilty conscience torments him, making him think that John the Baptist has come back to life with supernatural power. A guilty heart often turns fear and shame into terrifying thoughts.

Other people in the region suggest different explanations, saying Jesus is the prophet Elijah or one of the ancient prophets sent back to earth. People were eager to offer wild guesses rather than accept that Jesus was the true Messiah sent from God. Unbelief will accept almost any strange theory to avoid the truth.

When Herod hears these guesses, he insists that Jesus is John the Baptist, the very man he had beheaded. Herod had ordered John killed, and the memory of that crime still haunted his mind. A wicked person cannot silence the inward voice of a guilty conscience.

Mark explains that Herod himself had sent soldiers to arrest John and chain him in prison to please Herodias. Herod had unlawfully taken Herodias and married her, even though she was the wife of his living brother Philip. John was thrown into a fortress cell simply for speaking out against this sinful marriage.

John had repeatedly warned Herod that God's law forbade him from marrying his brother's wife. John was not afraid to speak the truth plainly to a king, even when it put his own life in danger. True servants of God stand up for what is right no matter who is offended.

Herodias held a deep, bitter grudge against John and wanted him executed. However, she could not carry out her wish because Herod kept stopping her. Unchecked anger often turns into a murderous desire to destroy anyone who points out our sin.

Herod protected John because he feared him, knowing that John was a holy and righteous man. Even though John's preaching made Herod feel deeply troubled and confused, the king still enjoyed listening to him. It is possible to respect God's truth and enjoy hearing it without ever giving up the pet sins that ruin the soul.

Herodias found her chance on Herod's birthday, when he threw a grand feast for his government officials, army commanders, and the leading men of Galilee. The palace was filled with the most important and powerful leaders of the area. Herodias used this lively celebration as a trap to bring about John's death.

Herodias sent her young daughter into the banquet hall to dance, and her performance thrilled Herod and his dinner guests. The king was so swept away that he told the girl she could ask for whatever she wanted, and he would grant it. Drunken revelry and foolish pride quickly lead people into making dangerous promises.

Herod confirmed his offer by making a solemn oath, swearing to give the girl whatever she asked, up to half of his kingdom. He made this reckless pledge in front of all his royal guests to make himself look generous and powerful. Making boastful vows in careless moments brings great regret.

The girl went outside to ask her mother what she should request, and Herodias told her to ask for the head of John the Baptist. Herodias seized this moment to wipe out the holy man who dared to challenge her unlawful marriage. Her bitter hatred proved more important to her than any wealth or worldly favor.

The girl rushed right back to the king and demanded that John the Baptist's head be given to her on a serving tray at once. She carried out her mother's cruel plan before the king had time to sober up or change his mind. Evil plans move quickly to strike before conscience can step in.

The king was deeply grieved, but he refused to say no because of his oath and the guests watching him at the table. He feared looking weak or foolish before his nobles far more than he feared murdering an innocent prophet. A sinful promise ought to be broken rather than kept by committing a worse crime.

Herod sent an executioner from his royal bodyguard with orders to bring back John's head. The soldier went directly to the dark prison cell and beheaded the holy prophet. Herod chose to slaughter an innocent servant of God just to protect his own pride.

The guard brought John's head on a platter and handed it to the young girl, who then gave it to her mother. Herodias received the dreadful prize she had plotted to get, gloating over the death of God's messenger. Wicked people may seem to win for a short time, but the death of God's holy servants is precious in His sight.
